The tenant portal
What a resident carries in their pocket, and the fifth tab their live-in manager sees on the same four tabs.
Out on the properties
The technician, the cleaning round, the leasing agent — and the one manager in this company who never gets a desk. Reactive work, a recurring round, a pipeline against a fixed date, and a team of four run from a phone.
The staff console
The four office roles that make a tenancy start, run and end correctly. They work at a desk, so they get a desk.
The exec portal
A different app for a different job: aggregates never people, exception-led, every figure badged with where it came from, and a scenario model that is a fork — it can read the whole operation and write to none of it.
The Berkeley Group · one page, three apps, nine roles, fonts embedded, nothing leaves this file.
Notes for reviewers. All names, amounts, requests, codes and registration numbers are fictional. Nine roles sit on this page. Switch between them above; All screens lays out every screen in all three apps at once.

Entry is always a notice, never a permission. Every entry carries at least 24 hours' written notice under Civil Code §1954, and the notice is informational — it records whether each occupant has seen it, and objections go through Messages so they are logged. Nothing in either app can grant or refuse entry, which settles the shared-room problem: one occupant of a triple cannot answer for two housemates. On the staff side the same rule is enforced arithmetically — the console computes the earliest lawful window and disables the rest, rather than trusting whoever is typing.

The three apps agree because they are the same rules seen from different chairs. A resident sees that a repair is coming today between 1 and 4; the dispatcher sees why no earlier window was lawful; the tech's Start button will not work before 1:00. A Community Assistant sees that a housemate is late; only Property Management sees by how much. A room's rent ceiling is derived from who still lives in it under Costa-Hawkins, never stored, so it cannot drift.

What isn't here, deliberately. No screen can revoke a door code for non-payment — not as a feature, not as a setting, not as an emergency override. There is no field anywhere for a Social Security number or citizenship status. A live-in manager cannot approve the identity of a person living down the hall, and an incident naming that manager leaves their hands the moment it is filed.

And nothing anywhere asks an applicant about criminal history. Berkeley's BMC 13.106 bans the question rather than the decision, so the application form has no field for it, no report is ordered that would return it, and no administrator has a switch that turns one on — the only reliable way to be certain a thing was never considered is to have had nowhere to put the answer. The leasing queue is ordered by receipt for the same reason: Berkeley permits a screening fee only where applications are worked in the order they arrive and the first qualified applicant takes the bed, so the order is the software rather than a policy somebody is trusted to follow.

Type. Display and figures are set in Crimson Pro, an oldstyle in the lineage of the face Frederic Goudy cut for the University of California Press in 1938. Labels use Arsenal SC small caps; interface text is National Park, drawn from US National Park Service signage; codes, clocks and ledger figures are DM Mono. All four are OFL-licensed and embedded in this file.
